tei:titleStmt.tei:title: עַל־מֹשֶׁה אֶרְגָּז וְאָהִים
Al Mosheh Ergaz v-Ahim — a pizmon on Mosheh's death for Simḥat Torah, by R. Shmuel ha-Dayan of Aram Ṣoba (ca. 12th c.)

tei:div.tei:head: Al Mosheh Ergaz v-Ahim — a pizmon on Mosheh's death for Simḥat Torah, by R. Shmuel ha-Dayan of Aram Ṣoba (ca. 12th c.)

tei:lg.tei:l: Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
The Concluder let him know Their wish —
The One who dwells in Their welkens and Their earth —
that his days were nearing and ending.
“Raise Your spirit to on high,
also return to God.”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
Moses called: “Not like a normal person
shall I die! Haven’t I previously the Presence
beheld, and heard a spoken word,
and took the luminous tablets
written with the finger of God!?”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
And the Rock on High said to him,
“From a land impure and bloody,
Get up and ascend to the lodge of the pure ones,
Who walk after Me and follow
and gaze upon God.”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
“How can I leave my scattered flock
From letting them know laws and Torahs?
And I set them as luminaries,
let their light not be puzzling.
I should trek with them to the house of God!”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
“Go, say no more words!
Get up and ascend to the Mountain of the Passing Ones,
and bury a body in the dust.
For you in the future a yearning people
will tell of the action of God.”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
Jochebed cried, and a bitter
fire was in her mind for Moses.
In pain, she trembled unspeaking.
“Bitter for you all, my loins are withered.
What angers God?”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
And she said, “I will deposit my child
into Your hand, the Only Judge.
You know the bitterness of my heart.
Place his travails among the luminous ones,
and in Eden, the garden of God.”
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
Amram’s son went to the partition.
No other racing man came to him.
He was taken with a kiss and was satisfied.
My loins shake and tremble for him.
Revealed to him was God.
Of Moses I am angered and shocked
that he was taken by God.
Today Israel sets
joy for the Torah, and is shocked
about Moses, and aloud shouts
They all weep and follow after
Moses, the man of God.

tei:note.tei:p: This translation for Shaddai is a reference to the midrash that interprets the name as meaning the One who said “that is enough” — she-dai. The idea of God as the one who sets boundaries is quite relevant to this poem about mortality.

This translation uses the pluralis majestatis to refer to the Divine. This is not meant to imply that God is more than one ḥas v’shalom but rather to reflect the vastness and majesty of God while also avoiding gendered language. See Ibn Ezra’s commentary on Genesis 1:1 for a discussion of the pluralis majestatis when referring to God.
Literally: “heart” — the seat of intellect and thought in Jewish folk practice.
Literally: “liver” — the seat of emotion and feeling in Jewish folk practice.
